/**
 * Extension for [ProxyHints.registerJdkProxy] providing a [KClass] based variant.
 *
 * @author Sebastien Deleuze
 * @since 6.0.5
 */
fun ProxyHints.registerJdkProxy(vararg proxiedInterfaces: KClass<*>) =
	registerJdkProxy(*proxiedInterfaces.map { it.java }.toTypedArray())
findings.explanation: The ProxyHints extension maps every KClass to its Java Class, preserving position and repeated occurrences, splats the resulting array into registerJdkProxy(Class<?>...), and returns that expression's result. The related JdkProxyHint.Builder extension performs the identical mapping into Builder.proxiedInterfaces(Class<?>...). Because the Java members return this, the extensions return the original ProxyHints and Builder receivers respectively; the bridges neither reorder nor deduplicate arguments. ProxyHintsExtensionsTests and JdkProxyHintExtensionsTests mock their receivers, stub the Class-varargs member to return the same mock, and verify calls with String::class.java followed by Int::class.java. This establishes conversion, overload handoff, and argument order only. The real Java bodies never execute, so those concrete/primitive example types do not prove acceptance; the real Class route rejects them because they are not interfaces.

The TypeReference-varargs overload delegates to this consumer overload with a callback that invokes Builder.proxiedInterfaces(TypeReference...), while the Class-varargs overload delegates with Builder.proxiedInterfaces(Class<?>...). Every invocation creates a fresh builder, invokes the callback, builds a completed hint, inserts it, and only then returns the same ProxyHints. The callback's own fluent Builder result is ignored. LinkedHashSet.add's boolean result is also ignored, so a successfully suppressed duplicate still returns the receiver. There is no catch or finally insertion: a callback/configuration exception or a build exception propagates immediately, insertion is not reached, no partially configured or newly completed hint is stored, and any hints already in the registry remain unchanged.

Every value supplied through the Class builder overload—including KClass values after bridging—must be an interface and must not be sealed. All invalid names are collected, then an IllegalArgumentException is thrown. Because proxiedInterfaces(Class...) evaluates this helper before calling addAll, failure occurs before any member of that batch is appended; earlier contents of a manually reused builder remain, but a registry registration still inserts nothing. Once validation succeeds, TypeReference.listOf streams the Classes in encounter order, maps each through TypeReference.of(Class), and that factory creates a ReflectionTypeReference. The direct TypeReference overload only appends its references and performs no interface, sealed-status, availability, or loadability check. It consequently accepts name-backed references to unavailable types and references representing concrete classes; even TypeReference.of(aConcreteClass) bypasses Class validation when passed through the TypeReference overload.

The builder holds a LinkedList. Each TypeReference call appends Arrays.asList(varargs), and each valid Class call appends the converted list. Calls accumulate in call and argument order; repeated interfaces remain repeated. Empty arrays append nothing, and a fresh or otherwise empty builder can successfully produce and register a hint whose interface list is empty. Construction uses List.copyOf, so the completed hint owns an unmodifiable snapshot; its getter exposes that immutable list, and later additions to the same builder affect only later builds. For the specified contract-violating case, a non-null TypeReference array containing null is first accepted by Arrays.asList and LinkedList.addAll. The builder method therefore returns normally, but List.copyOf rejects the null with NullPointerException during build. Through ProxyHints this happens after the callback and before set insertion, leaving no new stored hint.

A new builder's reachableType defaults to null and its boolean javaSerialization defaults to false. onReachableType assigns the supplied TypeReference and withJavaSerialization assigns the supplied boolean; both return the same builder, and repeated setter calls replace the prior value. Construction snapshots the then-current metadata, so later builder changes do not alter an existing hint. Equality requires the ordered, duplicate-sensitive interface list, reachable type, and serialization flag all to match. hashCode is intentionally narrower: it hashes only the interface list. Hints differing solely in reachability or serialization are therefore unequal but have the same hash; this is a legal collision and does not cause set deduplication.

The registry inserts completed hints into a LinkedHashSet, so its stream exposes first-unique-insertion order. An equal later hint is suppressed without replacing or moving the first; there is no sorting. Deduplication applies to the whole JdkProxyHint. Thus reordered lists, an added/removed repeated interface, or changed reachable/serialization metadata produce distinct hints, while the same repeated sequence and metadata deduplicate. Separately registered [A] and [A, B] hints both remain; their interface lists are never merged. Built-in Class-backed ReflectionTypeReference and name-backed SimpleTypeReference both inherit AbstractTypeReference equality against any TypeReference by canonical name and hash that same canonical name. Consequently, references produced by the built-in factories for the same type can compare and hash equally across those representations, allowing otherwise identical Class-based and name-based completed hints to deduplicate.
